c1-balanced-three-phase-power.studyNote: This derives constant total power for balanced sinusoidal loads. You can first study the worked P, Q and S examples below, then return to the trigonometric derivation.

c1-three-phase-power-factor.studyNote: Treat 4.8 kW as electrical input power. S = √3 × VL × IL is measured in VA, not W; power factor = P/S. Mechanical output requires a separate efficiency calculation.

c1-three-phase-line-current.studyNote: The 25 kW is electrical input power. Write apparent power as 31.25 kVA, although the narration says kW. If a motor rating gives shaft output, first divide it by efficiency.

c1-cable-design.studyNote: BS 7671 example: 15.7 kW is electrical input. Ib = 28.33 A; In = 32 A; required tabulated capacity ≈ 43.29 A. A table rating of 44 A is not installed Iz: 44 × 0.96 × 0.77 ≈ 32.52 A. Check terminal temperature limits, CPC, Zs and breaking capacity separately.

c1-three-phase-voltage-drop.studyNote: Follow the diagram values as captions can misread lengths. Express the balanced three-phase submain drop against line voltage and the single-phase final-circuit drop against phase voltage before adding percentages. An unbalanced feeder needs a fuller calculation.

c1-capacitor-sizing.studyNote: The available captions are badly corrupted, so this earlier resource is not the core calculation. Use the verified three-phase capacitor-bank lesson and the linked worked project for Qc = P(tan φ1 − tan φ2), units and a target power factor below unity.

c1-capacitor-placement.studyNote: Compare individual, group and central compensation. Specify switching, protection and discharge from manufacturer guidance. Automatic steps prevent overcorrection as demand falls. Do not connect correction capacitors to a VFD output.

c1-motor-terminals.studyNote: Study the nameplate first: a 230/400 V Δ/Y motor runs in star on a 400 V supply; a 400/690 V Δ/Y motor runs in delta on 400 V. A star–delta starter on 400 V needs a motor rated for delta running at 400 V and six accessible ends. Identify winding pairs on an isolated, disconnected motor.

c1-motor-protection-sizing.studyNote: Do not use the blanket 125% breaker rule as a BS 7671 or EPRA design rule. The kW example omits efficiency if kW means shaft output. Select protection from nameplate current, starting duty, cable protection and manufacturer coordination; distinguish relay range from its actual setting.

c1-phase-failure-relay.studyNote: Inspect the control diagram critically: protection in only the holding branch can be bypassed while Start is held. A validated protective contact must interrupt every energising path as required by the manufacturer. Do not copy this diagram as a complete approved control circuit.

c1-lost-neutral.studyNote: The RMS supply is approximately 230 V phase-to-neutral; its sinusoidal peak is about 325 V. Losing the shared neutral shifts the star point under unequal loads. Individual voltages depend on the impedances and can approach line voltage; they do not all become 400 V.

c1-trace-three-phase.studyNote: Apply only after safe isolation, proving dead and separating the conductors from all supplies and loads. Record each identified pair, verify the final conductor and remove temporary links before reconnection.

c1-motor-phase-loss.studyNote: Single-phasing can prevent starting or cause overheating while running. The quoted current multipliers illustrate a particular model; they are not universal trip settings. Compare phase currents, supply continuity and winding tests using the motor and protection manufacturer instructions.
